assumptions.ruleset: Gathering Storm with every expansion and the Leader Pass
assumptions.map: Continents or Pangaea, standard size, 8 civilizations
assumptions.notes: Turn numbers are Standard-speed scaffolding; the site rescales them for other speeds and difficulties. Pachacuti's single persona is planned here. The shape is Front-Load because the whole kit is mountains, the capital cannot be moved once planted, and every later city is either in the range or ordinary; the decisions that cap the game are made before the second Settler leaves.

verdict.one_line: Settle in the mountains, feed each city with Terrace Farms and domestic Trade Routes, put a Campus against three mountain faces in every city, and let the tallest cities on the map carry a Science game that Machu Picchu and mountain Universities accelerate.
verdict.why: Mit'a lets citizens work Mountains for two Production each, and Terrace Farms beside those mountains give the Food that lets a city work them; together they make the mountain city the tallest city type in the game, and tall cities with mountain-adjacent Campuses are Science. Qhapaq Ñan turns every domestic Trade Route into Food, so the range feeds itself without rivers or coast. Astronomy's Eureka comes from a University beside a Mountain, which every Inca Campus has, and Machu Picchu is a Classical wonder built on a mountain the Inca already work. Culture is the fallback because the same high-appeal mountain tiles make National Parks and Earth Goddess Faith; Domination is not in the kit because mountains slow your own armies as much as the enemy's.

must_have: A mountain range within three tiles of the start: at least three Mountain tiles workable from the capital, and hills touching them for Terrace Farms.
Room for four more cities along the same range, each with two or more Mountains in its first two rings, within domestic Trade Route range of the capital.
prefer: Hills beside the mountains rather than flat land: a Terrace Farm goes on a hill, and a hill next to two mountains is a four-Food tile from the first Builder.
Fresh water or a lake in the range for the capital's Aqueduct, which adds Production to every adjacent Terrace Farm.
Torres del Paine or Mount Kilimanjaro in the range; both double or feed Terrace Farms and raise appeal for Earth Goddess.
A second valley across a pass, so a Qhapaq Ñan can join two clusters and the empire keeps growing after turn 80.
map_check.no_go: No Mountain tile within four tiles of the start and no range visible on the horizon. Without mountains Mit'a does nothing, Terrace Farms are plain Farms, and Qhapaq Ñan is a Food trickle; the Inca are then a civ with a late Skirmisher and no ability.
map_check.fallback: If a range is visible but five or more tiles away, walk the Settler up to three turns toward it and settle on the first hill touching a Mountain; a late capital in the range beats an early one outside it. If nothing is visible by turn 4, settle in place, play a generic Campus-and-Commercial-Hub Science game, and say plainly that the kit is off; send the first two Settlers toward whatever mountains the Scout finds so that cities two and three carry the ability even if the capital does not.

kit_levers.name: Qhapaq Ñan
kit_levers.buys: Domestic Trade Routes carry extra Food for every Mountain tile adjacent to the origin city, and from Foreign Trade onward Builders can place the Qhapaq Ñan on Mountain tiles, a tunnel that moves units through the range and yields Food from the mountains beside it.
kit_levers.exploit: Every Trade Route this empire runs is domestic until the Industrial era: a route from a six-mountain city carries six Food and nothing a foreign route offers compares. The capital is sited to touch as many mountains as the map allows because it is the origin of the first three routes. The Qhapaq Ñan is laid across the pass between the two valleys so the second cluster is inside the empire's road net and not behind a wall.

kit_levers.name: Mit'a
kit_levers.buys: Citizens can work Mountain tiles for Production, and each Terrace Farm adjacent to a Mountain gains Food from it, so a mountain city feeds and builds itself from terrain other civilizations cannot use.
kit_levers.exploit: The Terrace Farm cluster is pinned before the first Builder moves: hills that touch two or more mountains, arranged so an Aqueduct tile can touch several of them. Citizens work Terrace Farms first for growth and Mountains second for Production; a 15-population mountain city at turn 120 works four mountains and seven Terrace Farms and out-builds a river capital.

kit_levers.name: Warak'aq
kit_levers.buys: A Skirmisher replacement that can attack a second time in the same turn if it still has Movement, which doubles its damage against anything that wanders into the valley.
kit_levers.exploit: Two of them per pass from Machinery onward are the whole defence: parked on a hill behind the mountain gap, each gets two shots before a Knight reaches the city. They are not an invasion force; the plan builds four and upgrades them, nothing more.

kit_levers.name: Terrace Farm
kit_levers.buys: A hill improvement that gives Food, Housing, extra Food for each adjacent Mountain, and Production from an adjacent Aqueduct and from neighbouring Terrace Farms.
kit_levers.exploit: The improvement decides city placement, not the other way round: a site is good if its first two rings hold four hills touching mountains. The Aqueduct is placed where it touches the most Terrace Farms, not where it is prettiest. Feudalism's Farm count and Serfdom's extra charges are spent on these before any Mine.

kit_levers.name: Sapa Inca
kit_levers.buys: Pachacuti likes leaders who leave the mountains alone and dislikes those who settle beside them.
kit_levers.exploit: Irrelevant to your own play. An AI Pachacuti on the map will resent any city of yours that touches a range; if he is a neighbour, settle your mountain cities first and his opinion follows.

turn_zero: Before the Settler moves: count the Mountain tiles within two rings of the start and the hills that touch them. Three mountains and two such hills is a go. Fewer than three mountains in sight means the fallback: walk toward the nearest visible range for up to three turns, or settle and run the plan from cities two and three.

Before the Settler moves: pick the tile that touches the most mountains while leaving the best mountain-adjacent hills free for Terrace Farms. The City Center cannot sit on a Mountain, and a center that uses up the one hill beside the range costs a four-Food tile for the game.

Before the Settler moves: pin the capital's Campus on the tile with the most mountain faces, the Aqueduct beside the Terrace hills, and the Holy Site or Theater Square second. The Campus tile is the one decision that cannot be improved later.

By turn 10: draw the range. Every city site along it within Trade Route range of the capital, each with its Campus tile and its Terrace cluster marked, and the pass where the Qhapaq Ñan will go. Cities one through six are decided now; the Scout only confirms them.
front_load.ceiling: Six to eight cities along one or two ranges, each reaching 15 to 20 population on Terrace Farms and domestic Food, each with a Campus at +3 or more from mountains alone. That is a Science victory around turn 270 on Emperor from Universities beside mountains, Rationalism in every city, and Spaceport projects in the two tallest. Early Production is the cap: a mountain city builds its first districts slowly, so the plan supplements it with Mines on the Terrace-free hills and the Ancestral Hall's Builders. The empire is tall and compact, not wide; it cannot out-settle a flat neighbour and does not try.

irreversibles.decision: Capital tile: how many mountains it touches sets the Food on every domestic Trade Route for the game, and the Campus tile beside it sets the capital's Science.
Terrace Farm cluster and Aqueduct tile pinned in the capital. A Mine or a district on a hill that touches two mountains removes a Terrace Farm for good.
The range map: cities two through six, each on a hill touching mountains, each with its Campus tile named. A city founded off the range for its river has no Mit'a Production and feeds no route.
Which pass gets the Qhapaq Ñan and which Builder lays it; the second valley is either joined by turn 60 or settled 30 turns later than the plan needs.

front_load.settle_map_rule: Draw every city before the second Settler is produced. A site qualifies if it sits on a hill or flat tile touching at least two Mountains, has four or more hills touching Mountains in its first two rings for Terrace Farms, and lies within domestic Trade Route range of the capital or of a city already drawn. Mark the Campus tile for each site as the one with the most mountain faces and the Aqueduct tile as the one touching the most Terrace hills. A river or coast is a bonus and never a reason; a site with a river and one mountain is skipped for a dry site with three. Cities six and seven may be beyond a pass; they are drawn now, with the Qhapaq Ñan tile that reaches them, so the first Builder in the second valley knows where it is going.

phases.name: Assess and commit
phases.objective: Settle against the range, pin the Campus, the Aqueduct and the Terrace Farm cluster, draw the range map for cities two through six, found the pantheon, and have the second Settler out and the first Terrace Farms built by turn 20. The twenty turns that decide the game.

Archery from the first barbarian kill, and a ranged unit in the pass while the Warriors are away.

City three toward the second valley, so the Qhapaq Ñan has somewhere to go.
On the pinned tile the turn Writing lands; three mountain faces is +3 before any building.

checkpoints.fail: Fewer than three mountains: run the fallback and plan to carry the kit in cities two and three. Terrace hills unpinned: pin them this turn, before the Builder places a Mine on one.

checkpoints.fail: No map yet: draw it this turn, before the Settler moves. A Mine on a Terrace hill: leave it, strike the hill from the cluster, and pin a replacement.

Pin the Campus on the most-mountain tile, the Aqueduct beside the Terrace hills, and mark every hill touching two Mountains as a Terrace Farm.
Scout along the range both ways; mark the pass, the camps, and the sites that match the drawn map.
First Builder places three Terrace Farms on the pinned hills; Craftsmanship collected on the third.
Draw cities two through six along the range, each with its Campus tile and Terrace cluster named, and the Qhapaq Ñan tile across the pass.
Found Earth Goddess, or Stone Circles if the valley holds two Stone quarries and little appeal.

Low decision density; the work is following the range map.

decision_triggers.name: A site has a river and one mountain
decision_triggers.if: The next drawn site is dry with three mountains and a better-looking river site with one mountain sits two tiles away.
decision_triggers.then: Take the dry site. The Aqueduct and the Terrace Farms supply the Housing and the Food; the river supplies nothing Mit'a does not, and a one-mountain city feeds a one-Food route.

decision_triggers.name: An army enters the valley
decision_triggers.if: A rival force appears at a pass before turn 150.
decision_triggers.then: Do not build Walls in the inner cities. Two Warak'aq on the hill behind the gap fire twice each per turn; the pass city's own ranged attack finishes what they leave. Pillaged Terrace Farms are repaired by the next Builder.

decision_triggers.name: Production stalls
decision_triggers.if: At turn 60 the capital takes more than twelve turns per district.
decision_triggers.then: Expected for a mountain start and already planned for: switch two citizens from Terrace Farms to Mountains, buy a Builder for Mines on the spare hills, and send an envoy to the Industrial city-state. Do not chop; there is nothing to chop.

decision_triggers.name: The second valley is contested
decision_triggers.if: A rival Settler is seen heading for the sites beyond the pass before the Qhapaq Ñan is laid.
decision_triggers.then: Send the next Settler through on foot with a Warrior and settle the far site first; the pass is laid afterward. Losing the valley caps the empire at five cities; walking costs ten turns.

abort.trigger: Turn 20 with a capital touching fewer than two Mountains and no range reached by city two, or turn 80 with three or more cities off the range.
actions: Say plainly that the Inca are an ordinary civ this game and stop planning Terrace clusters that do not exist.
Play a generic Science game: Campuses by whatever adjacency the land gives, Commercial Hubs for Gold, Rationalism, and the Spaceport in the best Production city.
Keep the domestic Trade Route habit anyway; even one or two mountains at a city is Food nobody else gets.

fail_state: Turn 120 with six cities at eight population, Mines on the hills that should have been Terrace Farms, Campuses placed beside rivers for the Commercial Hub rather than against the mountains, and the second valley settled by a rival. The decisions that caused it were made before turn 20 and no improvement or district can be moved.
common_mistakes: Mining a hill that touches two Mountains because the city needs Production now. That hill is a four-Food Terrace Farm for the game; the Production comes from working the Mountain beside it.
Running foreign Trade Routes for Gold. The leader ability is on domestic routes only; a six-mountain origin city sends six Food, which is a Granary and a half per route.
Settling beside the river instead of against the range. Mit'a and Qhapaq Ñan do nothing for a river city; the Aqueduct gives the Housing the river would have.
Placing the Campus where the Commercial Hub wants to be. The Campus takes the tile with the most mountain faces, always; the Commercial Hub gets Machu Picchu's adjacency later.
Building an army to use the Warak'aq. It attacks twice because it is a pass guard; four of them is the whole military and the mountains do the rest.
sources: Civilization VI Civilopedia, Gathering Storm ruleset (Inca, Pachacuti, Terrace Farm, Qhapaq Ñan, Warak'aq, Machu Picchu).

Where the civ-info text differs from the game, the game is followed: the Warak'aq's edge is a second attack per turn when it has Movement left, not higher Ranged Strength; Mit'a's mountain Production is a flat yield and the plan does not rely on an Industrial-era increase; Terrace Farms count toward the Feudalism Inspiration as Farms.
